title.en: Your first day: names, time and word order

summary.en: Introduce yourself and say that today is your first day.

body.en:
Titus opens with *Ja, ich bin Titus.* — “Yes, I’m Titus.” To introduce yourself, use *Ich bin* and your name. The two words identify the speaker before the name is given. The form *bin* belongs to *sein*, even though the written forms look quite different.

*Heute ist mein erster Tag hier.* means “Today is my first day here.” A German statement can begin with a time expression. The finite verb stays in the second position: *Heute ist …*. A position can contain a whole phrase; it does not mean the second written word in every sentence.

*Tag* is masculine. After *mein*, the describing word carries the masculine nominative ending: *mein erster Tag*. The possessive identifies whose first day it is. The ending belongs to the noun phrase; it is not chosen because of the speaker’s gender.

The word *hier* means “here”, the workplace in this scene. Compare *Mein erster Tag ist heute.* — “My first day is today.” That new practice sentence uses only words from the scene, with the focus shifted from the time to the first day. It is not extra dialogue attributed to the programme.

Replay the introduction once for the name and once for the first-day phrase. Keep those phrases together while listening, then use the word drawer to compare the individual forms.
